Based on the healthcare Q&A matches, it appears that delayed diagnosis of anorectal malformations (ARM) can be attributed to several factors. Current guidelines, as mentioned in some of the retrieved matches, may not be sufficient to ensure prompt diagnosis.

One study found that ARM occurs in approximately 32% of patients referred to the institution over a period of 2.5 years. This suggests that delayed diagnosis is indeed common.

In another match, linear anorectal endosonography was found to demonstrate incomplete or even absent relaxation of the anal sphincter and the m. puborectalis during a defecation movement in most patients with dyschesia (a condition characterized by abnormal relaxation of the anal sphincter). This highlights the potential value of this ultrasonographic technique in diagnosing "pelvic floor dyssynergia" or "anismus."

It is also mentioned that vitamin D deficiency treatment in Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) patients with ergocalciferol can be inadequate, as current guidelines are not sufficient to correct both VDDI and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Further research is needed to explore the effects of higher or more frequent dosing of ergocalciferol on these clinical endpoints.

Regarding diagnosis and follow-up in constipated children, using ultrasound (US) is recommended to make a correct diagnosis and monitor progress objectively. This can also reassure patients and families that treatment should continue.

Finally, there are questions about the radiographic transition zone correlating with the level of aganglionosis on the specimen in Hirschsprung's disease. The findings suggest that this correlation remains low, emphasizing the need for systematic preoperative biopsy by coelioscopy or ombilical incision.

In conclusion, delayed diagnosis of anorectal malformations can be attributed to various factors, including current guidelines and inadequate treatment of vitamin D deficiency in CKD patients with ergocalciferol. The use of ultrasound, diagnosis and follow-up in constipated children, and the relationship between radiographic transition zone and aganglionosis in Hirschsprung's disease all highlight the importance of prompt detection and effective management of these conditions.
